scope: Complete multi-jump capture sequences for men (A64-014.4): terminal sequences only, the Turkish-strike rule that a taken piece stays standing and cannot be taken again, path revisits, maximum-capture filtering, and both configured mid-sequence promotion rules. Standalone king movement is still absent; the only king here is one a man became mid-sequence.

cases.description: Landing on e5 puts the man beside a second victim, so the ply is not over: only the complete c3xe5xg7 is offered, never the c3xe5 prefix.
Three jumps in one ply. Neither the one-jump nor the two-jump prefix appears, which is what makes every generated capture safe to hand straight to MoveApplier as a whole ply.

Russian draughts obliges a capture but lets the player choose which, so a one-piece sequence stands beside a two-piece one. The maximum-capture filter is disabled here; the same position under international rules is the next case.

The same four pieces on a 10x10 board. International draughts obliges the largest capture, so the one-piece sequence is filtered out after the search — never pruned during it, since a branch that opens small can finish largest.

A ring of four victims. The man goes round it either way, ends back on the square it started from — c3 appears twice in the path — and stops because every remaining neighbour is a piece it has already taken. Without the taken-once rule the walk would circle forever. The two sequences are the same length, so this also pins the order between equals.

Landing on d8 crowns the man, and it carries on jumping as a flying king — reaching e7 from d8 and coming down on f6, which the light man on g5 stops it passing. A man could not have made the second jump, so this fails outright if crowning waits until the ply ends.

The same shape under international rules: f10 is the crownhead and the man crosses it without being crowned, finishing on h8 as a man. The contrast with the Russian case above is configuration, not a variant check in the walker.
The other half of the international rule. Passing over the crownhead is not promotion; stopping on it is.
